title: Relief valves
calcLabel: Open the relief valve sizing tool

steps.q: What sets the highest set pressure allowed for a vessel's single relief valve?
steps.title: Pressure ladder
steps.summary: A single relief valve is set at or below the vessel's maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP). Normal operating pressure is kept below about 90 % of set pressure so the valve does not simmer and leak. While relieving, pressure may rise above MAWP by the allowed accumulation: 10 % for a single valve in a non-fire case and 21 % for the fire case.

steps.title: Thermal relief
steps.summary: Liquid trapped between closed valves expands when it warms, more than the steel pipe does, so the pressure can climb by several bar for each degree. A small thermal relief valve releases a few drops to stop gaskets and flanges failing. Route its outlet to a tank or closed drain.

opts.t: The pipe shrinks in the heat

steps.q: A relief valve discharges into a header with varying back pressure. Which type suits it?
steps.title: Back pressure
steps.summary: In a conventional spring-loaded valve, back pressure acts on the disc and changes the opening pressure, and it reduces capacity. Where back pressure varies, as in a shared header, a balanced bellows valve shields the disc so the set point stays put; keep the bellows bonnet vent open and routed to a safe place, since gas there means the bellows has failed. A conventional valve is usually limited to built-up back pressure of about 10 % of set pressure.

steps.q: A rupture disc sits under a relief valve. Why is there a pressure gauge between them?
steps.title: Disc + valve
steps.summary: A rupture disc under a relief valve keeps corrosive or sticky process away from the valve and stops leakage. A disc bursts on the pressure difference across it, so a pinhole that lets pressure build in the space between disc and valve makes it burst late. A pressure gauge or tell-tale in that space shows it is at zero; check it on every round.

opts.t: To spot a pinhole leak in the disc

steps.q: Can you fit an isolation valve under a relief valve on a process vessel?
steps.title: Isolation valves
steps.summary: Isolation valves under relief valves are allowed so a valve can be removed for testing without a shutdown, but a closed one leaves the vessel unprotected. They must be full bore, locked or car-sealed open and listed on a register, and closed only under a permit with a spare relief valve in service, or a person posted full time who can stop the pressure source. Steam boiler safety valves must never have an isolation valve under them.

steps.q: A relief valve chatters: it slams open and shut again and again. What is the likely cause?
steps.title: Chatter
steps.summary: Chatter is rapid opening and closing. If the inlet pipe loses too much pressure when the valve flows, the pressure at the disc falls below the reseat point, the valve slams shut, pressure rebuilds and it reopens. An oversized valve chatters for a similar reason. Keep inlet pressure loss below 3 % of set pressure and size the valve for the real relieving flow.

opts.t: The set pressure is too high

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: relief valves, the last thing standing between a vessel and the sky. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now try the relief valve sizing tool.

q1.text: Question 1. What sets the highest set pressure allowed for a vessel's single relief valve?

q1-r0.text: Set it at operating pressure and it'll pop every afternoon.

q1-r1.text: Yes! The vessel's maximum allowable working pressure.

q1-r2.text: Twice? The vessel might not be built for that.

q1-r3.text: The pump is one cause of overpressure, not the limit.

q1-b0.text: Start with the vessel's maximum allowable working pressure, the MAWP. A single relief valve is set no higher than this.

q1-b1.text: Operating pressure sits well below it, usually under 90 percent of set, or the valve simmers and leaks.

q1-b2.text: When it relieves, pressure can rise a little above MAWP. That's accumulation: 10 percent for a single valve.

q1-b3.text: For a fire case, the code allows 21 percent above MAWP, because a fire is a rare, short emergency.

q2.text: Question 2. A liquid-full pipe, blocked in at both ends, sits in the sun. Why fit a small relief valve?

q2-r0.text: It doesn't need to boil. It only needs to warm up a little.

q2-r1.text: Correct! Trapped liquid, a few degrees warmer, huge pressure.

q2-r2.text: Air can't get into a blocked, liquid-full pipe.

q2-r3.text: Pipes grow in the heat, not shrink. And the liquid grows faster.

q2-b0.text: Close both valves on a liquid-full line. Now the liquid has nowhere to go.

q2-b1.text: Liquid expands as it warms, more than the steel does. With no space to expand into, pressure climbs fast.

q2-b2.text: A few degrees of sun can blow a gasket or crack a flange. A small thermal relief valve lets a few drops out.

q2-b3.text: Route it somewhere safe: back to a tank or a closed drain, not onto a walkway.

q3.text: Question 3. A relief valve discharges into a header with varying back pressure. Which type suits it?

q3-r0.text: A conventional valve's opening point moves when back pressure changes.

q3-r1.text: Yes! The bellows takes the back pressure off the disc.

q3-r2.text: A gate valve is for isolation. It doesn't relieve anything.

q3-r3.text: A check valve only stops reverse flow. It won't save the vessel.

q3-b0.text: In a conventional valve, back pressure pushes on top of the disc and adds to the spring.

q3-b1.text: So when the header pressure changes, the valve opens at the wrong pressure, and its capacity falls too.

q3-b2.text: A bellows shields the disc from the outlet side. Back pressure no longer changes the opening point. Keep its bonnet vent open and routed safely: gas there means the bellows has failed.

q3-b3.text: Rule of thumb: a conventional valve copes with built-up back pressure up to about 10 percent of set.

q4.text: Question 4. A rupture disc sits under a relief valve. Why is there a pressure gauge between them?

q4-r0.text: The vessel has its own gauge. This one has a different job.

q4-r1.text: Yes! A pinhole lets pressure build up behind the disc.

q4-r2.text: Valves are set on a test bench, not with this gauge.

q4-r3.text: Nothing on a relief line is decoration.

q4-b0.text: The disc keeps corrosive or sticky process away from the valve, and stops it leaking.

q4-b1.text: A disc bursts on the pressure difference across it. A pinhole lets pressure build up in the space between the disc and the valve.

q4-b2.text: Now the disc needs the vessel pressure plus that trapped pressure to burst. It opens late.

q4-b3.text: So the gauge, or a tell-tale, shows the space is at zero. Check it every round.

q5.text: Question 5. Can you fit an isolation valve under a relief valve on a process vessel?

q5-r0.text: On a steam boiler, never. On a process vessel the codes allow it, with conditions.

q5-r1.text: Correct. Locked open, with a procedure for closing it.

q5-r2.text: Any valve? One wrong turn and the vessel has no protection.

q5-r3.text: The fluid doesn't decide it. The control does.

q5-b0.text: Valves under relief valves let you remove one for testing without a shutdown.

q5-b1.text: But a closed one leaves the vessel with no protection at all.

q5-b2.text: So they must be locked or car-sealed open, full bore, and on a register.

q5-b3.text: Close one only under a permit, with a spare relief valve in service, or a person posted full time who can stop the pressure source. And never on a steam boiler.

q6.text: Question 6. A relief valve chatters: it slams open and shut again and again. What is the likely cause?

q6-r0.text: A high set point makes it open late, not chatter.

q6-r1.text: Yes! The valve starves and slams shut. An oversized valve does it too.

q6-r2.text: A stronger spring just raises the set point.

q6-r3.text: A big vessel helps keep the pressure steady, if anything.

q6-b0.text: The valve opens, and flow rushes through the inlet pipe.

q6-b1.text: If the inlet loses too much pressure, the pressure at the disc drops below reseat. It slams shut, the pressure builds again, and it reopens.

q6-b2.text: An oversized valve does the same: there's not enough flow to hold it open.

q6-b3.text: Keep the inlet loss under 3 percent of set pressure, and size for the real flow. Check yours with the relief valve sizing tool on pharmacheme dot in.
